opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest hope is pretty simple to say: we want inference to become something nobody has to think about. Today, if you want to serve a large model well, you need a team that understands GPU kernels, memory management, scheduling, distributed parallelism, and all the quirks of each new hardware generation. That's a huge barrier. Over the next ten years I'd like Inferect to help turn that complexity into infrastructure, the way electricity or cloud storage became infrastructure. You just plug in and it works, and it's cheap.

Cost is really the core of it. In the last couple of years the price per token has dropped by orders of magnitude, and every time it drops, new applications show up that weren't economical before. Agents that run for hours, models that read entire codebases, reasoning models that think for thousands of tokens before answering, all of these are fundamentally bottlenecked by inference cost and latency. So if we can keep pushing that curve down by another few orders of magnitude, I think we unlock a whole class of things we can't even imagine yet.

The second thing is openness. Coming from the open-source inference community, I've seen how much faster the whole field moves when the serving layer is shared. Model developers, hardware vendors, and application builders can all meet at a common layer instead of everyone rebuilding the same stack in private. I'd like Inferect to strengthen that ecosystem rather than replace it, so that a new chip or a new model architecture can be supported in days rather than months, and the benefits flow to everyone.

And longer term, I think inference and training will blur together. Models will keep learning from their interactions, systems will be co-designed with the model architectures, and the line between "serving" and "improving" a model will get thinner. If in ten years people look back and say the inference layer was one of the reasons AI became truly widespread and affordable, and that we played a real part in that, I'd be very happy.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the hope is to make inference something nobody has to think about, turning its complexity into cheap, plug-and-play infrastructure. This communicates inference becoming essentially solved.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I think about ten years, the first thing I want to say is that I hope inference becomes boring. That sounds strange coming from someone who started a company around it, but let me explain what I mean.

Today, running a large model efficiently is still a craft. You need people who understand the hardware, who understand the model architecture, who know which kernel to pick, how to batch requests, how to manage the KV cache, how to split a model across machines. That knowledge is concentrated in a small number of people, and a lot of it is tribal. When I was working on vLLM, every week there was some new trick, some new quantization scheme, some new attention variant, and the whole community had to scramble to support it. That's exciting for engineers, but it's a sign that the field is immature.

So what I hope for over ten years is that inference becomes infrastructure in the way electricity or networking is infrastructure. You don't think about TCP when you open a web page. I want a developer to pick a model, or train their own, and have it run close to the physical limits of whatever hardware they have, without hiring a team of systems experts. That means the layer between the model and the chip has to become much smarter and much more automatic than it is now.

There are a few concrete things underneath that. One is hardware diversity. Right now a lot of the world's inference runs on one vendor's GPUs, and that's not healthy, economically or technically. In ten years I expect there will be many more kinds of accelerators, including a lot coming out of China, and the software layer has to make those genuinely usable, not just nominally supported. That's a big part of what I want Inferect to do, to be the layer that makes new hardware first-class from day one rather than two years later.

The second is cost. If you look at the price per token over the last few years, it's dropped by orders of magnitude, and I think that trend continues. But most of that drop so far has come from the models getting smaller and from hardware getting better. The system software layer still has a lot of room. Better scheduling, better memory management, disaggregating prefill and decode, speculative decoding done well, serving many models and many adapters on shared hardware. I think there's another ten to a hundred times available just from systems work, and I'd like us to be the ones who find it.

The third thing, and maybe this is the one I care about most, is that I want the whole thing to stay open. The reason vLLM worked is that it was open source and people everywhere contributed. Hardware vendors, cloud providers, researchers, students. If inference infrastructure in ten years is a closed box owned by two or three companies, I think that's a loss for everyone, including the model developers. So part of my hope for Inferect is that we can build a sustainable company while keeping the core open, and show that those two things aren't in conflict.

If I had to compress it into one sentence, I'd say I hope that in ten years, anyone with a good idea for a model can get it in front of users at the cost of electricity, on whatever hardware is available to them, without needing to know anything about what we did. If we succeed, nobody will talk about us, and that's fine with me.

r001.rationale: He says he hopes inference becomes “boring” infrastructure that runs efficiently without requiring systems experts, conveying his aim to make it a basically solved problem.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that Inferect will make large-model inference affordable and reliable enough to become everyday infrastructure. Building a powerful model is only part of the challenge; people also need to run it at a cost and speed that make sense for their applications.

Over the next ten years, I’d like us to reduce the complexity involved in doing that. Developers should be able to focus on what they want to build without having to become experts in hardware and inference optimization. If we can help more people turn useful ideas into practical applications, that would be a meaningful achievement.

r001.rationale: The response says Inferect should make inference affordable, reliable, and simpler to use, but does not clearly identify bringing large-model inference to a basically solved state as the ten-year hope.

sol-6.1.text:
My hope is that Inferect can make large-model inference efficient, affordable, and easy to use. Over the next ten years, I’d like us to help close the gap between what models can do and what people can actually deploy, especially when they have limited hardware or a tight budget.

That means looking beyond a single performance benchmark. Latency, throughput, cost, and reliability all matter, and different applications need different trade-offs. I hope we can make those choices easier for developers, so they can spend more time building useful applications and less time managing inference infrastructure.

Ultimately, I’d be happy if the technology became something people could take for granted: models responding quickly, running reliably, and being accessible to many more people.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they hope inference becomes something people can take for granted, with models responding quickly and running reliably. This communicates bringing large-model inference to a basically solved state.
